source.title: Epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries in Brazilian American football: associations with pre-activity routines, sleep, and mood

paper.citation: Marques Dias N., Martins T.B., Raulino Silva May E., De Menezes F.S., Beppler Martins T., Okubo R. Epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries in Brazilian American football: associations with pre-activity routines, sleep, and mood. Research in Sports Medicine. 2026;:1-16. doi:10.1080/15438627.2026.2673042.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What is the self-reported musculoskeletal-injury profile of Brazilian American-football players, and are injury histories associated with individual characteristics, training and game habits, pre-activity routines, sleep, or mood? Participants: 60 adult male athletes, mean age 30.3 ± 6.9 years, from a convenience sample recruited in Brazil. Sport and level: Active Brazilian American-football players spanning positions and amateur or semi-professional contexts. Design: Retrospective, cross-sectional observational epidemiology study conducted August–October 2025. Exposure or intervention: Self-reported training/game volume, pre-activity routines, sleep symptoms, mood, and other athlete characteristics; no intervention.
paper.tldr: Thirty-three of 60 athletes reported at least one injury in 2024–2025, giving a self-reported prevalence of 55.0%; 93 total injuries were reported, with a median of 2.0 injuries per injured athlete. Estimated incidence was 7.26 injuries per 1,000 hours overall, 18.59 per 1,000 game-hours, and 1.36 per 1,000 training-hours; these rates use retrospectively estimated exposure rather than prospective attendance records. The strongest use of this paper is to inform what a prospective surveillance system should measure: verified exposure, injury context, anatomical region, mechanism, severity/time loss, recurrence, preparation routines, sleep, and mood.
paper.methods: Design: Retrospective, cross-sectional observational epidemiology study conducted August–October 2025. Exposure or intervention: Self-reported training/game volume, pre-activity routines, sleep symptoms, mood, and other athlete characteristics; no intervention. Comparator: Injured versus non-injured respondents. Measurements and outcomes: Author-developed online questionnaire; injuries broadly defined as sport-related musculoskeletal complaints causing pain, functional limitation, or time loss; BRUMS mood scale and adapted Mini Sleep Questionnaire. Analysis: Descriptive statistics, estimated injuries per 1,000 exposure-hours, t tests, chi-square or Fisher tests, and a post hoc power calculation.
paper.findings: Thirty-three of 60 athletes reported at least one injury in 2024–2025, giving a self-reported prevalence of 55.0%; 93 total injuries were reported, with a median of 2.0 injuries per injured athlete. Estimated incidence was 7.26 injuries per 1,000 hours overall, 18.59 per 1,000 game-hours, and 1.36 per 1,000 training-hours; these rates use retrospectively estimated exposure rather than prospective attendance records. The most frequently affected regions among injured athletes were ankle/foot (42.4%), knee (39.4%), shoulder/clavicle/arm (33.3%), thigh (30.3%), and wrist/hand/fingers (30.3%). Strains were reported by 54.5% and sprains by 42.4% of injured athletes; multiple responses were allowed, so these percentages are not proportions of all 93 injury events. Injured athletes were taller than non-injured athletes (180.8 ± 6.3 versus 176.0 ± 6.8 cm, p = 0.007), while age, body mass, playing experience, and weekly training/game volume did not differ significantly. No tested categorical variable—including position, unit, training level, additional activity, or pre-training/pre-game routine count—was significantly associated with injury occurrence.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional retrospective self-report introduces recall bias and may overrepresent severe injuries while missing minor or transient conditions. Injuries were not necessarily clinically confirmed, and the broad complaint-based definition differs from standardized prospective surveillance definitions. Exposure was calculated from self-reported average training/game time rather than verified athlete-exposures or participation minutes. The convenience sample was small, heterogeneous by position and competitive level, and may have been underpowered for smaller associations. Sleep and mood symptoms were described, but the reported inferential table did not establish them as injury predictors; athlete beliefs about sleep or warm-up are perceptions, not causal evidence. Brazilian amateur/semi-professional infrastructure, age distribution, and exposure differ materially from NCAA American football, so absolute rates should not be imported into Baylor benchmarks.
paper.practicalImplications: The strongest use of this paper is to inform what a prospective surveillance system should measure: verified exposure, injury context, anatomical region, mechanism, severity/time loss, recurrence, preparation routines, sleep, and mood. It does not justify screening athletes by height or claiming that warm-up, sleep, or mood caused the observed injuries. For collegiate practice, local prospective data with standardized definitions and medical verification should remain the decision source.
